name: CagriSema

lead: CagriSema is a once-weekly injection combining semaglutide with cagrilintide, an amylin analogue. People chasing large fat loss discuss it, sometimes alongside retatrutide, for the lower body fat and leaner look that comes with substantial weight loss.

Semaglutide activates GLP-1 receptors and cagrilintide activates amylin receptors; both reduce appetite through partly different pathways. A phase 3a trial in adults without diabetes found about 20% mean weight change over 68 weeks versus about 3% with placebo. It beat semaglutide alone in a meta-analysis of early trials, and in a developer-reported head-to-head trial it did not meet non-inferiority against tirzepatide.

paras: Novo Nordisk is developing it as a weekly injection for adults with overweight or obesity, with or without type 2 diabetes. It is used within clinical trials, and a new drug application was filed with the US FDA in December 2025.
Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea and constipation are the most reported effects, and were more frequent than with semaglutide alone. It has no approved label, and any supply outside trials is unregulated.

angle.text: CagriSema is a weekly cagrilintide and semaglutide shot used by people after large fat loss, sometimes compared with retatrutide. The two drugs cut appetite through different pathways, lowering body fat. Phase 3 trials showed about 20 percent weight loss in people with obesity; it is not approved.

lead: CagriSema is an investigational once-weekly injectable combination of cagrilintide, an amylin receptor agonist, and semaglutide, a GLP-1 receptor agonist, developed by Novo Nordisk for weight management [1][2]. It is intended for adults with overweight or obesity, with or without type 2 diabetes, and is not an appearance product in itself; any effect on looks comes through fat loss.

In a phase 3a trial in adults without diabetes, the combination produced a mean body-weight change of about 20% over 68 weeks versus about 3% with placebo [1][3]. A meta-analysis of three early randomized trials found greater weight loss with the combination than with semaglutide 2.4 mg alone, together with more gastrointestinal adverse events [2]. In a head-to-head open-label trial reported by the developer, it did not meet the non-inferiority endpoint against tirzepatide [1].

Per Grokipedia, a new drug application was filed with the US FDA in December 2025, and the product was not approved at the time of that source [1]. In forum discussion, CagriSema is mentioned alongside other newer peptides such as retatrutide [4].
infobox: Amylin receptor agonist + GLP-1 receptor agonist (fixed combination)

paras: The studied use is chronic weight management in adults with obesity, or with overweight plus a weight-related condition, with or without type 2 diabetes [1][3][5]. Separate phase 3 programs have also examined its effects on blood glucose in type 2 diabetes and on blood pressure [6][7][8]. Registered trials include studies in adolescents with type 2 diabetes, people with hypertension and obesity, and weight-loss maintenance [9][10][11].

A phase 2 trial in type 2 diabetes tested the coadministration of cagrilintide 2.4 mg and semaglutide 2.4 mg against each agent alone [12]. In the 68-week phase 3a REDEFINE 1 trial in adults with overweight or obesity, CagriSema was compared with placebo and with each component alone [3]. Grokipedia reports a change of -20.4% versus -3.0% with placebo, and about 80% of participants with gastrointestinal adverse events [1]. A companion trial in adults with type 2 diabetes (REDEFINE 2) is reported there to have shown smaller weight reductions, around 15.7% versus 3.1% on placebo [5][1]. A blood-pressure analysis of REDEFINE 1 has also been published [7].

A 2024 meta-analysis of three randomized trials with 430 participants reported a mean difference of about -9 percentage points in weight versus semaglutide 2.4 mg at 20-32 weeks, with high heterogeneity; gastrointestinal events and vomiting were higher with the combination [2]. Phase 3 REIMAGINE trials in type 2 diabetes have been published in 2026 [6][8]. Recent network meta-analyses and reviews place CagriSema among next-generation obesity drugs expected to achieve weight loss in the range of tirzepatide [13][14][15][16][17].

In the REDEFINE 4 open-label head-to-head trial against tirzepatide 15 mg, as reported by Grokipedia, weight loss was 20.2% to 23.0% with CagriSema versus 23.6% to 25.5% with tirzepatide, and non-inferiority was not met [1]. Ongoing registered trials include a 2,500-person phase 3 study and a trial of switching from semaglutide [18][19].

The reported adverse-event profile resembles that of the GLP-1 class: nausea, vomiting, diarrhea and constipation, mostly mild to moderate [1][2]. Grokipedia reports about 6% discontinuation for adverse events and injection-site reactions in about 12% of users [1]. Since the product is unapproved, no official label or contraindication list exists.

Semaglutide activates GLP-1 receptors and cagrilintide acts on amylin receptors; amylin is a hormone co-secreted with insulin that influences satiety and postprandial glucose [20][16]. Reviews describe combining hormones with complementary actions as a strategy to increase weight loss beyond GLP-1 agonism alone [14][15]. Grokipedia reports a 16-week dose-escalation period [1].

Because CagriSema is unapproved, any use outside trials would be of unregulated product. Posts in a T Nation thread group it with retatrutide and other research peptides that users describe positively [4]. Regulators have not authorized it for sale.

lore.intro: CagriSema appears only briefly in community discussion, usually as an upcoming or research-grade successor to semaglutide, listed beside retatrutide [4].
